title: THE BIBLE PUT A SUSPECTED WIFE ON TRIAL—BUT NUMBERS 5 IS NOT SAYING WHAT THE INTERNET TOLD YOU
paragraphs:
THE BIBLE PUT A SUSPECTED WIFE ON TRIAL—BUT NUMBERS 5 IS NOT SAYING WHAT THE INTERNET TOLD YOU
Numbers 5 contains one of Scripture’s strangest rituals: a jealous husband, an accused wife, holy water, dust, an oath, and a terrifying appeal to God. But hidden beneath this disturbing scene is a truth about accusation, guilt, innocence, judgment—and eventually Jesus Christ—that is far more unsettling than the controversy surrounding the passage.
There is a woman standing before the priest.
Her marriage is bleeding.
Her husband suspects her of adultery.
But there is a problem.
He cannot prove it.

No eyewitness has stepped forward. No ordinary judicial case can settle what has happened. Suspicion has entered the marriage, and suspicion is a terrible thing because it can destroy a home whether it is true or false.
Maybe she betrayed him.
Maybe she did not.
Maybe he is right.
Maybe he is horribly wrong.
And that uncertainty is precisely where one of the strangest passages in the Old Testament begins.
Numbers 5:11–31 describes what is often called the ordeal of the suspected adulteress, traditionally associated with the Hebrew term sotah.
Read it quickly and the passage can sound primitive, humiliating, even horrifying.
Read it through arguments on social media and you may be told something even more specific:
“The Bible contains a ritual abortion.”
“The priest gives a pregnant woman something that causes miscarriage.”
“Numbers 5 proves God commanded abortion.”
But slow down.
Before defending Scripture, attacking Scripture, quoting Scripture, or turning Scripture into ammunition for another argument, Christians have an obligation to do something much less exciting.
Actually read what it says.
Not what a meme says.
Not what a preacher wishes it said.
Not what an opponent of Christianity claims it says.
The text.
And when we do, something remarkable happens.
The passage remains uncomfortable.
It remains ancient.
It remains severe.
But some of the most popular claims about it begin falling apart.

Numbers 5 introduces a situation in which a husband believes his wife has been sexually unfaithful, but the alleged act has not been established through witnesses. The woman is brought before the priest and, ultimately, symbolically placed before the LORD.
That distinction matters.
The husband does not simply announce her guilt and punish her.
His jealousy is not the verdict.
His suspicion is not proof.
His emotional certainty does not become judicial certainty.
He must surrender the matter to a process in which the outcome belongs to God.
That is already more significant than many readers notice.
Because human beings are frighteningly good at confusing suspicion with knowledge.
We have done it in marriages.
Churches.
Families.
Friendships.
We see something.
We hear something.
Someone sends us a screenshot.
Someone whispers a story.
And suddenly suspicion becomes certainty.
Certainty becomes accusation.
Accusation becomes condemnation.
And sometimes a person's reputation is dead before anyone bothers asking whether the accusation was true.
Numbers 5 does not permit the husband's jealousy to function as evidence.
The matter is brought before God.

The priest takes holy water in an earthen vessel and places dust from the tabernacle floor into it. The woman is placed under oath. Words of the curse are written and washed into the water. She drinks what Scripture calls the “water of bitterness.”
The Hebrew calls it:
מֵי הַמָּרִים הַמְאָרֲרִים
mei hammārim ham'ārərim
The water associated with bitterness and the curse.
But notice what is not described.
There is no identifiable abortifacient listed.
There is no recipe for terminating a pregnancy.
And most importantly, the passage never tells us that the woman is pregnant.
That fact alone should make us careful about confidently calling the ritual an “abortion.”
Then we reach the words at the center of the controversy.
Numbers 5:27 describes the consequence if the woman really has been unfaithful:
וְצָבְתָה בִטְנָהּ וְנָפְלָה יְרֵכָהּ
wetṣāḇəṯāh ḇiṭnāh wənāfelāh yərēḵāh.
The first expression is comparatively straightforward.
בֶּטֶן — beten
can refer to the belly, abdomen, body, or womb depending upon context.
וְצָבְתָה — wetsavtah
describes swelling.
Her abdomen or belly swells.
Then comes the much more debated expression:
וְנָפְלָה יְרֵכָהּ
Literally, something like:
“and her yarek falls.”
יָרֵךְ — yārēḵ can refer to the thigh, loin, side, or the region associated with the reproductive body.
That is why translations differ.
Some English translations render the language in ways that readers associate with miscarriage. Others use language such as the thigh wasting, falling, or shriveling.
We should therefore say neither more nor less than Scripture allows us to say.
The text describes a catastrophic bodily judgment associated with the abdomen and the yārēḵ if the woman is guilty.
It may involve reproductive consequences.
It certainly concerns bodily judgment.
But the Hebrew does not simply say, “her unborn baby will miscarry.”
The Hebrew wording is more difficult than that.
And the next verse makes the picture even more important.
Numbers 5:28 says of the innocent woman:
וְאִם־לֹא נִטְמְאָה הָאִשָּׁה וּטְהֹרָה הִוא וְנִקְּתָה וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע
Wə'im-lō niṭmə'āh hā'iššāh, uṭəhōrāh hî; wəniqqəṯāh wənizrə'āh zāraʿ.
If the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, she is cleared and can “be seeded with seed”—an idiomatic expression connected with conception or offspring.
In other words, the passage contrasts judgment upon actual covenant unfaithfulness with vindication and fertility for the woman who is innocent.
That is very different from the simplistic claim that Numbers 5 gives priests instructions for performing abortions.
But perhaps you are thinking:
“That explains the Hebrew. It still doesn't make the passage comfortable.”
Correct.
It shouldn't.
We make a serious mistake when we believe biblical faithfulness means pretending difficult passages are not difficult.

Numbers 5 comes from an ancient covenantal and judicial world very different from ours. The ritual belongs to Israel's life under the Mosaic covenant, with the tabernacle, priesthood, purity regulations, sacrificial system, covenant sanctions, and God's unique presence among His covenant people.
Christians are not instructed to recreate this ritual.
No pastor should prepare bitter water because a husband suspects his wife.
No church should imitate the ordeal.
The passage belongs to the covenantal world in which God was teaching Israel about holiness, adultery, truth, judgment, purity, and His presence among them.
And yet there is something buried in this strange scene that reaches directly into our lives.
Because Numbers 5 is not merely about a suspicious husband.
It is about something we desperately want to avoid.
The possibility that God knows what human beings cannot see.
Think about that.
The husband does not know.
The community does not know.
The priest does not possess supernatural investigative powers.
But God knows.
There are sins no spouse discovers.
Search histories nobody sees.
Messages deleted before anyone reads them.
Affairs hidden behind business trips.
Pornography buried beneath respectable Christianity.
Financial deceit concealed inside a marriage.
Private flirtations defended as harmless.
Bitterness disguised as discernment.
Lust disguised as loneliness.
Pride disguised as conviction.
Gossip disguised as prayer requests.
Religious performance disguising a heart that has wandered miles away from Jesus.
We have become experts at deleting evidence.
But there is no delete button before God.
That is where Numbers 5 stops being an archaeological curiosity and starts becoming uncomfortable.
Because the deepest terror of the passage is not bitter water.
It is divine knowledge.
The accused woman stands before God because the truth cannot finally remain hidden from Him.
And neither can ours.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been fighting.
Maybe your husband doesn't know.
Maybe your wife doesn't know.
Maybe your parents don't know.
Maybe your pastor doesn't know.
Maybe the people who follow you online think your spiritual life is stronger than it actually is.
Maybe you know exactly how to lift your hands during worship while hiding something you would be terrified to place in the light.
There are things we hide from people because we fear what will happen if they discover them.
But Scripture relentlessly confronts us with a God from whom nothing is concealed.
And this is where the story could become unbearable.
Because if God sees everything...
and God is holy...
and we are guilty...
then what hope is left?
This is where the Bible does something astonishing.
It takes us from an accused woman standing before a priest...
to another scene.
Another accusation.
Another judgment.
Another curse.
Another person standing before religious authorities.
Jesus Christ.
Except Jesus was not secretly guilty.
He was completely innocent.
The New Testament uses the Greek word:
ἀναμάρτητος — anamartētos
“without sin” or “sinless.”
Jesus was not merely a better person than everyone around Him.
He was the spotless Lamb.
The innocent One.
And yet the innocent One was condemned.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Spat upon.
Nailed to wood.
Why?
Because the Gospel is not the story of God pretending guilt doesn't matter.
The Gospel is the story of guilt mattering so much that redemption required the cross.
Paul writes that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.
Read that slowly.
The curse.
For us.
The One without adultery bore judgment for adulterous hearts.
The One without deceit bore judgment for liars.
The One without lust bore judgment for the sexually broken.
The One without greed bore judgment for thieves.
The One without hypocrisy bore judgment for hypocrites.
The One without secret sin carried the sins we hoped nobody would ever discover.
Numbers 5 confronts us with a terrifying truth:
God knows.
Calvary confronts us with an even greater one:
God knew...
and Christ came anyway.
That does not make sin small.
It makes grace enormous.
Jesus did not go to the cross because your sin was harmless.
He went because it wasn't.
Grace is not God shrugging at adultery.
Grace is not God pretending betrayal doesn't destroy people.
Grace is not permission to keep living secretly while posting Bible verses publicly.
Grace calls us out.
Grace brings us into the light.
Grace tells the adulterer to repent.
Grace tells the liar to tell the truth.
Grace tells the porn-addicted believer to stop hiding.
Grace tells the bitter Christian to forgive.
Grace tells the self-righteous Christian that respectable sins still required blood.
Grace looks directly at the scandal...
and offers a Savior.
Maybe that is why this strange passage matters more than we realized.
We entered Numbers 5 asking:
“What happens to the suspected woman?”
And somehow Scripture turns the question around.
What happens when God examines me?
Not my profile.
Not my reputation.
Not the Christian version of myself that everyone else sees.
Me.
The thoughts.
The motives.
The secret compromises.
The private wounds.
The things I did.
The things done to me.
The sins I confessed.
The sins I renamed so I wouldn't have to confess them.
The places where I have been falsely accused.
And the places where I really am guilty.
That distinction matters too.
Because perhaps you relate to the woman in Numbers 5 for a completely different reason.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be suspected of something you didn't do.
To have someone interpret your silence as guilt.
To have your character questioned.
To watch a rumor outrun the truth.
To realize that you cannot force everyone to believe you.
There is something profoundly relevant here:
God knows innocence too.
The God who sees hidden guilt also sees hidden faithfulness.
He knows when people lied about you.
He knows when you were misunderstood.
He knows when the screenshot lacked context.
He knows when the accusation was false.
He knows what happened in the room when nobody else was there.
You do not have to manufacture guilt where God knows innocence.
And you do not have to manufacture innocence where God knows guilt.
You can come into the light.
Because for the Christian, the final answer to guilt is not pretending.
It is Jesus.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for entertainment.
Repentance is surrendering the exhausting project of hiding from the One who already knows.
And perhaps someone reading this has been hiding for years.
You love Jesus.
At least you say you do.
But there is a locked room in your heart where you don't let Him speak.
You keep feeding something you know is killing your intimacy with God.
You keep telling yourself:
“Tomorrow.”
“After this season.”
“When life gets easier.”
“When I'm stronger.”
“When nobody will get hurt.”
But tomorrow keeps moving.
And the chains keep tightening.
Listen carefully.
You do not need better camouflage.
You need Christ.
You do not need a more believable excuse.
You need repentance.
You do not need to become worthy enough to crawl back to God.
You need to come home through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Confess.
Turn.
Ask forgiveness.
Make restitution where restitution is biblically necessary.
Seek wise pastoral help where the situation requires it.
Bring the secret into appropriate, trustworthy light.
Not because exposing sin saves you.
Jesus saves.
But the Jesus who saves sinners does not call us to become more sophisticated at hiding sin.
He calls us to follow Him.
And if you have fallen badly, hear this:
Your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your life.
Peter denied Jesus.
David committed grievous sin and suffered devastating consequences.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly disgraced.
Paul had blood attached to his former way of life.
The Gospel never says their sins did not matter.
It says grace was greater.
That is Christianity.
Not scandal erased by pretending it never happened.
Scandal met by truth.
Truth met by repentance.
Repentance met by mercy.
Mercy purchased by Christ.
And a ruined story placed into the hands of the only Author capable of writing redemption into the next chapter.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to tell strangers every detail.
But perhaps you do need to stop pretending.
There is no shame in admitting that you need prayer.
There is danger in deciding you no longer need repentance.

And if someone came into your mind while reading this—someone fighting temptation, someone whose marriage is hurting, someone who has been falsely accused, someone drowning in shame, someone who thinks their scandal has disqualified them from grace—send this article to them.
Somebody may need to discover that Christianity does not offer camouflage for sinners.
It offers Christ to sinners.
Numbers 5 will come up again.

Someone will claim that the passage clearly says something the Hebrew does not clearly say, and you may need to return to the actual words rather than repeating whichever interpretation happens to fit your side of an argument.
Truth deserves better than that.
Scripture deserves better than that.
And Jesus deserves disciples who care about what God's Word actually says.

Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as a substitute for obedience, generosity to your local church, caring for your family, serving the needy, prayer, repentance, or personally sharing Christ.
Grace cannot be bought.
And there is much more available even without paying.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to earn His blessing.
Not because clicking “share” proves your faith.
Do it, if you choose, because truth worth receiving is truth worth passing on.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend quietly drifting from God.
Invite the believer who needs Scripture more than another motivational quote.
Invite the skeptic willing to investigate Christianity honestly.
Jesus Christ.
Because Numbers 5 ultimately leaves every one of us with a question much larger than the controversy surrounding bitter water.
If the God who sees everything looked into the hidden chambers of your life tonight...
what would He find?
And when He finds what you hoped nobody would ever see...
will you run farther into the darkness?
Or finally run toward the Savior who already knew?
The most shocking thing about Christianity is not that God discovered your scandal.
It is that He knew the whole story before the cross—and Jesus still opened His arms.
